PMCID: PMC13636137
TITLE: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis: Plant-Based Therapy for Irritable Bowel Syndrome.
PUBLICATION TYPES: ["Meta-Analysis", "research-article", "Systematic Review", "Journal Article"]
ARTICLE TYPE: research-article
ABSTRACT:
ABSTRACT Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common disorder of brain‐gut interaction that presents with abdominal pain, bloating associated with variable stool consistency. Many IBS patients prefer plant‐based preparations to pharmacological therapy; however, the utility of this approach is not well established. To address this issue, a systematic review with meta‐analysis to assess the efficacy and safety of plant‐based therapy in IBS patients was performed. Literature search with 3 electronic databases (Medline via PubMed, Embase via Ovid, and Web of Science Core Collection) from inception to May 2024. Efficacy was assessed using dichotomous ratings of change in IBS symptoms. A random effects model with 95% confidence intervals was used. Through the screening process, 60 eligible studies were identified (6329 patients). Meta‐analysis was performed for fiber (8 studies, RR = 1.22; 95% CI: 1.00–1.49), peppermint oil (7 studies, RR = 1.63; 95% CI: 1.33–2.00), Aloe vera (3 studies, RR = 1.25; 95% CI: 0.76–2.06), and Chinese herbal medicine (7 studies, RR = 1.56; 95% CI: 1.27–1.92). For other plant‐based substances investigated in at least one randomized controlled trial (RCT) (e.g., St. John's wort, Anise oil), there were insufficient data for a meta‐analysis. The quality of many studies was limited. The findings demonstrate that the treatment of IBS patients with peppermint oil and Chinese herbal medicine were more effective than placebo and had a good safety profile. Dietary fiber showed effects that approached significance. Further, well‐powered RCTs are needed to establish the place of plant‐based preparations in IBS treatment.
METHODS:
2 Materials and Methods The description of the methods is based on the PRISMA guidelines (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and meta‐analyses) (Rethlefsen et al. 2021 ; Page et al. 2021 ). A protocol for this systematic review was published on Prospero ( https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_record.php?ID=CRD42022322137 ). 2.1 Selection Criteria Prospectively defined criteria for inclusion and exclusion were applied. Randomized controlled trials (RCT) that included standard therapy or placebo as comparators were included. Standard therapy for IBS differs between different geographical regions and centers and has changed over time; however, one can generalize that, in addition to diet and lifestyle recommendations, standard medical therapy for IBS includes preparations to regulate stool consistency and frequency (e.g., PEG, imodium) and also the use of spasmolytics to treat abdominal bloating and spasm (e.g., hyoscine butylbromide [Buscopan], pinaverium [Dicetel]) (Layer 2021 ; Fox et al. 2018 ). Additionally, other clinical trials without a control group that fulfilled the inclusion criteria were included in the systematic review, as long as more than 10 subjects participated. This decision was made because we wished to review the full range of plant‐based preparations that has been subjected to study. For a study to be included, the diagnosis of IBS had to be established either by widely used criteria (e.g., Manning, Manning et al. 1978 ; Rome criteria, Mearin et al. 2016 ), or medical diagnosis of IBS. The latter was accepted because this diagnosis is often made in primary care without the use of formal criteria, and plant‐based preparations are often applied in this setting. Clinical outcome was assessed in terms of improvement in IBS symptoms on the plant‐based intervention. Assessment tools included, for example, the IBS symptom severity score (Francis et al. 1997 ). Forced choice questions about “adequate relief of abdominal pain and discomfort” (Mangel et al. 1998 ) or reported change in symptoms such as abdominal pain or bowel movements were also accepted. As above, this decision was made to include as wide a range of studies as possible. Exclusion criteria included homeopathic medicines (D3 or greater), unpublished or only partially published studies, patients under 18 years of age, studies with fewer than ten participants, and publications in languages other than German or English. In case of lack of access to the full texts or insufficient information in the publications, the authors were contacted. 2.2 Search Strategy A comprehensive literature search was initially run on 30th March 2022 and then rerun on 6th May 2024 in the following electronic databases: MEDLINE (PubMed), EMBASE (Ovid) and Web of Science Core Collection (Clarivate Analytics). Prior the execution of the search strategies developed by AM, these were peer reviewed. by an information specialist (LCO) using the PRESS (Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies) checklist (Lefebvre and Duffy 2021 ). The search was limited to clinical trials of humans and no date or language limitations were applied. The reproducible search strategy for MEDLINE (PubMed) is available in Table 1 . Search results were deduplicated using the Bramer method in EndNote (Bramer et al. 2016 ; Bramer and Bain 2017 ). 2.3 Screening The citations were screened by AM and NS independently at the level of title and abstract. The full texts were then further screened for their suitability to be included in this systematic review. Both steps were performed in Covidence, a software application designed for systematic reviews that allows multiple reviewers to work independently of one another and in a blinded manner without knowledge of the other's decisions. At the full text screening stage, a reason was given for each study if it was excluded. In case of disagreement, consensus was sought through discussion, and the results were cross‐checked by the senior author MF. 2.4 Data Extraction Data were summarized in tables according to the following aspects: General information: Author and year of publication, country in which the study was conducted, study design and treatment duration. Patient population: total number of study participants, drop‐out, age, sex, IBS definition and IBS subgroup. Study characteristics: plant‐based preparations, dosage, control, endpoints, adverse effects and outcome. A data extraction template was created in Covidence which AM and NS completed independently, and the results were cross‐checked by the senior author MF. Disagreements were resolved by consensus. 2.5 Risk of Bias Assessment The Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool was applied as advised by the Cochrane Collaboration (Sterne et al. 2019 ). The following domains were assessed for each study: Bias risk from the randomization process, from deviations from the intended interventions (effect of allocation to the intervention), from missing outcome data, from outcome measurement, and from selection of the reported outcome. This checklist was completed by AM and NS independently in Excel and the result transferred to Covidence. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus. 2.6 Meta‐Analysis A meta‐analysis was conducted for each preparation. The effectiveness rates in the intervention group compared to those in the comparator group were expressed as relative risk. This was recorded dichotomously as improvement or remission of IBS symptoms (thresholds defined in the original publications). A random effects model with 95% confidence intervals was applied (DerSimonian and Laird 1986 ). If RR > 1.0, then the therapy was more effective than placebo. If the confidence interval did not include 1.0, the intervention was significantly different to placebo. The number needed to treat with 95% confidence interval was calculated (NNT = 1 / (assumed control risk × [1—RR])). Heterogeneity between studies was assessed with the Chi‐square ( χ 2 )‐test. A p ‐value < 0.10 was used to define significant heterogeneity. The I 2 statistic was also used to test for heterogeneity among the included studies. A value between 0% and 24% did not indicate heterogeneity; 25%–49%, 50%–75%, and > 75% represented low, medium, and high heterogeneity, respectively (Higgins et al. 2003 ). Forest plots were generated using Review manager, version 5.4.1 (The Cochrane Collaboration 2020). Funnel plots were to be assessed for signs of asymmetry. However, more than 10 studies had to be available for this (Sterne et al. 2011 ). In addition, a possible publication bias was to be determined using Eggers' test (Egger et al. 1997 ).
